judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 1056, which limits who can inherit a commercial gill net or trammel net permit. California stopped issuing new ones long ago, so these permits change hands only by transfer. The law removes the rule that let a permit pass to another qualified fisher when the holder died or became disabled. From January 1, 2027 a long-standing holder may pass a permit only to a family member, and once it moves that way it cannot be passed on again. It passed the California State Assembly 51-17 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 1061, which narrows a historic-buildings rule that had been keeping small housing projects and lot splits out of fast-track approval. Before, any site inside a listed historic district was shut out; now only a building that actually contributes to such a district, or a property listed as a landmark in its own right, is. Cities and counties may still set clear standards to protect the character of a district on the state historic register. judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 524, which makes every police agency set rules for official reports written with artificial intelligence. Such a report must say that a computer helped write it and carry the signature of the officer who prepared it, and the first computer-written draft must be kept as long as the report. It passed the California State Assembly 50-17 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 704, which requires gun barrels to be sold or handed over in person through a licensed gun dealer. The rule does not cover sales to police agencies, the military, licensed dealers, or collectors of antique guns. It also leaves out transfers from someone's estate, a barrel already attached to a gun, and a barrel bought in the same sale as a gun that gets its own background check. Holding barrels with plans to sell them is also barred unless the seller is a licensed dealer. From July 1, 2027 the dealer must check whether the buyer is allowed to own a gun, for a fee of up to $5, and keep a record of the sale. A first or second offense is a misdemeanor, and later ones can be charged as felonies. It passed the California State Assembly 57-20 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 246, the Social Security Tenant Protection Act, which lets a tenant being evicted over unpaid rent point to a break in their Social Security payments as a defense, through January 20, 2029. It covers income lost because something the federal government did, or failed to do, stopped, delayed, or reduced the benefits the household normally receives. A tenant who satisfies the court of that, and that it is why the rent went unpaid, has the eviction put on hold. The hold ends at whichever comes first: 14 days after the benefits start again, or six months. The rent is still owed, and within 14 days of the money resuming the tenant must pay everything behind or agree a payment plan with the landlord. It passed the California State Senate 27-11 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 518, which sets up a Bureau for Descendants of American Slavery inside the state Civil Rights Department, run by a deputy director the governor appoints and the Senate confirms. judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 634, which stops cities, counties, and special districts from passing or enforcing local laws against people who help the homeless. No local law may stop a person or organization from providing support services, or from helping someone with the basics of staying alive. That means help with eating and drinking, sleeping, staying out of the weather, and staying clean and healthy, including handing out food, water, blankets, and pillows. It does not cover handing out plywood or other heavy building materials. The state calls this a statewide matter, so it binds charter cities too. It passed the California State Assembly 55-20 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 1037, which widens access to overdose-reversal drugs such as naloxone. Standing prescriptions and the right to carry one now cover any overdose, not only an opioid overdose, and anyone in a position to help a person at risk may hold one and pass it on. It drops the rule that a person be trained before receiving or carrying one. Someone who gives the drug in good faith, and is not paid for it, is generally not liable for civil damages, trained or not, unless they were grossly negligent or acted wilfully. It passed the California State Senate 30-10 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 627, which makes it a crime for a law enforcement officer to wear a face covering that hides who they are while on duty. The rule reaches federal agents and officers from other states working in California, and the offense is an infraction or a misdemeanor. Officers may still cover their faces while working undercover, during tactical operations, where health and safety law requires it, to protect their identity during a prosecution, or as a disability accommodation. Every agency working in the state must post a written face-covering policy by July 1, 2026, and officers whose agency posts one that follows the law cannot be charged. It passed the California State Assembly 45-23 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 628, which adds a working stove and refrigerator to the things a rented home must have to be fit to live in, for leases signed, changed, or renewed from January 1, 2026. If the maker or the government recalls a stove or refrigerator, the landlord has 30 days from being told to repair or replace it. A tenant and landlord may agree when signing that the tenant will supply and look after their own refrigerator, on conditions the law sets. Some homes, including permanent supportive housing, are left out, and tenants keep their existing rights to fix a problem themselves or move out. It passed the California State Senate 25-11 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 858, which keeps a job recall law running until January 1, 2027. It covers hotels, private clubs, event centers, airport food and service companies, and the firms that clean and maintain office and retail buildings. judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 1319, which makes it illegal in California to bring in, send out, carry, sell, buy, or hold for sale any fish, wildlife, or plant taken in breach of a state or federal wildlife law. It measures those laws as they stood on January 19, 2025, so later cuts to federal protection do not narrow it, and anything seized is forfeited on conviction. The Department of Fish and Wildlife must also add a species to a temporary candidate list when federal protection for it is reduced. The rules stop working at the end of 2031, and a business is not liable while it follows a federal permit that allows some harm to a protected species. It passed the California State Senate 25-10 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Assembly Bill 692, which bars employers from making a worker sign a contract, from January 1, 2026 on, that leaves the worker owing money if the job ends. These stay-or-pay deals can require paying back an employer, a training company, or a debt collector. Some are still allowed: government loan-repayment programs, tuition for a credential the worker can take to another job, approved apprenticeships, certain signing bonuses, and contracts to rent or buy a home. A banned term counts as an illegal restraint on a person's right to work, and a worker can sue over it, for themselves or for others in the same position, and collect penalties. It passed the California State Senate 25-11 and became law.

Those employers must tell workers they laid off about openings the workers are qualified for, and offer the jobs in an order of preference. It protects workers with at least six months on the job who were laid off for reasons tied to the COVID-19 pandemic, and bars punishing a worker for claiming these rights. The California State Assembly agreed 49-19, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 596, which tightens the fines hospitals face for breaking nurse-to-patient staffing limits. A hospital escapes a fine if it has used up its on-call list of nurses, and the law now spells out what that list is. Calling nurses who were not scheduled on call, and who are not in the backup pool for that ward and shift, does not count as using it up. The health department must also treat a breach on each separate day as its own violation. It passed the California State Assembly 48-19 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to agree to the Assembly's changes to Senate Bill 763, which raises the top fines for illegal deals that restrain trade under California's antitrust law. A company can now be fined up to $6 million, up from $1 million, and a person up to $1 million, up from $250,000, or more if the court ties the fine to the money made or the losses caused. The law also adds a penalty of up to $1 million for each violation, which the Attorney General or a district attorney can seek in a civil case. The California State Senate agreed 29-8, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to agree to the Assembly's changes to Senate Bill 42, the California Fair Elections Act, which lifts the state ban on candidates using public money to run for office. Only candidates who accept spending limits and meet the qualifying rules could take it. Public money could not pay legal bills or pay a candidate back for loans to their own campaign, and the fine for taking money from a foreign government goes up. Because the bill changes a law the voters passed, it takes effect only if voters approve it at the election on November 3, 2026. The California State Senate agreed 29-8, sending the bill to the governor, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 73, which bars police officers from interfering with the running of an election and lets named officials sue to enforce that. No one may let a law enforcement agent see, disturb, change, or take voter rosters or voter lists without a court order, unless they are investigating certain voting fraud. For certified voting machines the rule is stricter: a court order is needed, with no fraud exception. Under either rule, officers may still help with logistics, transport, or security if the elections official has signed a written agreement with their agency. The Attorney General must publish guidance on answering law enforcement requests to enter rooms where ballots are kept. Taking a package of voted ballots from an elections official is now a crime, and an observer may not challenge a signature the voter has already confirmed. It passed the California State Assembly 57-19 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 567, which repealed Missouri's earned paid sick time law in full, the law voters approved as Proposition A in November 2024. judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Joint Resolution 73, which would repeal the reproductive-freedom right Missouri voters added to the state constitution in 2024. It would allow abortion only for a medical emergency, a fetal anomaly, rape or incest, and only through 12 weeks of pregnancy in cases of rape or incest. It would let the legislature regulate abortion providers and facilities, bar public funding except for a medical emergency, rape or incest, and require consent from both a minor and a parent. It would also ban gender transition surgery, cross-sex hormones and puberty blockers for anyone under 18. The Missouri House passed it 103-51. It takes effect only if Missouri voters approve it; a joint resolution needs no governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 71, which made it burglary in the second degree to break into a motor vehicle or into a restricted area of a commercial business, and a class C felony when a firearm is involved or stolen. It created a new class A misdemeanor for trying the handles of one vehicle after another to get in and steal. It required fingerprint-based state and federal criminal background checks for applicants to about forty licensing boards and for peace officer training. It also let public retirement systems close records tied to their investments and business dealings, and let the local government retirement board debate investments in closed session. It dropped the rule that that board's investment counselor be registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The Missouri House passed it 112-33 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 595, which stopped Missouri cities and counties from passing several kinds of renter protection. They may no longer bar a landlord from refusing a tenant because the tenant's lawful income includes housing assistance. They may no longer limit how a landlord uses income tests, credit scores, credit reports, eviction or property damage history, or criminal history. They may no longer cap a security deposit or require that tenants get a right of first refusal. Cities and counties may still bar discrimination against people who receive veterans' benefits, and they keep their authority over property they own, voluntary subsidized-rent agreements and homes assisted with federal community development block grant money. A separate section requires a real estate broker acting for a buyer or tenant to sign a written agency agreement before acting, not while acting. The Missouri House passed the conference version 103-37 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 594, which cut personal income tax by letting individuals deduct 100 percent of their capital gains starting with the 2025 tax year. The same deduction reaches corporations only if Missouri's top individual income tax rate first falls to 4.5 percent or less. The bill also exempted diapers, incontinence products and feminine hygiene products from state sales tax, and raised and inflation-indexed the property tax credit for seniors and disabled veterans. It let counties, ambulance districts and fire protection districts ask their own voters for higher local sales taxes. The Missouri House adopted the Senate's version 102-41 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 145, which closed several kinds of government records under Missouri's Sunshine Law. It closed individually identifiable information about minors held by cities, towns, villages and park boards, and the customer usage and billing records of municipal utilities. It also closed camping and lodging reservation details for public parks and the locations of endangered or imperiled species. Names, billing addresses and service dates for commercial utility accounts stay public. The bill widened the officials who can have their personal information stripped from public records to include prosecutors' employees, court clerks and juvenile officers. It also lets an agency treat a records request as withdrawn if the requester does not pay the fees within 90 days, or 150 days when the fees top $1,000. The Missouri House gave it final approval 107-50 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 152, which barred foreign nationals from funding or steering Missouri ballot measure campaigns. A foreign national may not contribute to, spend on, give in-kind support to, solicit money for, or take part in the decisions of a committee working on a ballot measure. Committees must get a written affirmation from anyone giving more than $2,000 that the donor is not a foreign national. Violators can be ordered to refund or hand over the money, committee officers can be held personally liable, and damages can reach twice the amount, or three times that for a knowing violation. The Attorney General enforces the new sections, and the law switches off the Missouri Ethics Commission's usual complaint process for them. It also gives donors to tax-exempt organizations a right of privacy that limits what the Attorney General may collect or disclose. The Missouri House passed it 94-47 and it became law.
